Protection de la jeunesse —
132260

2013 QCCQ 20771

JL4031

COURT OF QUEBEC

Youth
Division

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUEBEC

DISTRICT OF

[…]

N° :

525-41-026245-126

DATE:

June 4th, 2013

______________________________________________________________________

PRESIDING JUDGE :

THE HONORABLE

CLAUDE LAMOUREUX, J.C.Q.

______________________________________________________________________

In
the matter of :     X

Born
on:                  [...], 2004

The Director of Youth Protection A

applicant

-
and -

A,
the mother

- and -

B, the father

respondents

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

(section 38 Y.P.A.)

______________________________________________________________________

WARNING:
The Youth Protection Act prohibits the publication or
broadcasting of any information that may lead to the identification of a child
or his parents.  Any person who contravenes this provision commits an offence
and is liable to fine.
[
Y.P.A. sections 11.2.1
and 135
]

[
1
]

As required under Section 90 of the Youth
Protection Act, the present judgment confirms in writing the decision taken
under advisement at the hearing held on May 1
st
, 2013.

[
2
]

The Court is seized with a motion under section
38 of the Youth Protection Act requesting that the security or development of
the child

be declared to be in danger for the following reasons:

3.1.      the situation of the child has been
signalled since she was exhibiting concerning sexualized and aggressive
behaviours at school;

3.2.      in fact, the child was talking about sexual
elements she was quite young to be aware of, and would engage her schoolmates
in sexual play;

3.3.      the child also tried to harm herself a few
times, by using scissors, swallowing papers, etc.;

3.4.      due to the extent of her sexualized
behaviours and her aggressiveness towards her peers, a shadow had to accompany
her in school;

3.5.      the child's behaviour also deteriorated at
home such as urinating on her pillows or in the cat's litter box, vandalizing
the neighbour's balcony by smearing soot and charcoal all over, etc.;

3.6.      the child also attempted to engage her five
year old brother in sexual experimentation;

3.7.      on or about June 21
st
, 2012, the
child disclosed that she had been sexually abuse;

3.8.      the child disclosed that her father and his
ex-girlfriend would have such sexual intercourse in front of her and would ask
the child to participate, which she did;

3.9.      the child also reported that she would take
her shower with the father's ex-girlfriend whom she was forced to wash;

3.10.    the father's ex-girlfriend's daughter would
simulate having sex with the child;

3.11.    it is relevant to mention that the child has
not seen her father for approximately one (1) year since the mother has been
made aware that he had been suspected of having sexually assaulted his
ex-girlfriend's daughter;

3.12.    during the time the child was visiting her
father, he was consuming cocaine and there were concerns regarding conjugal
violence between the father and his partner at the time;

3.13.    there are pending charges for sexual assault
against the father with his ex-girlfriend and the trial is scheduled for
October 19
th
, 2012;

3.14.    the father's collaboration with the Director
of Youth Protection is minimal and the child needs immediate intervention,
assessments and care, for which father is not giving his consent, failing to
meet with the Director of Youth Protection delegate;

[
3
]

The Director is recommending that the child be
maintained in her mother's care, that there be an interdiction of contact with
the father, along with aid, counsel and assistance and other corrective
measures, the whole for a period of one year.

[
4
]

The mother, assisted by Me Brunet, consents to
the measures proposed by the Director.

[
5
]

The father, represented by Me Bourdeau, was
never present. Through his lawyer, he consents to the measures proposed by the
Director.  Me Bourdeau underlined the fact that the evidence suggests that the
child wants to see her father and that contacts should be allowed if service
providers (Centre A) so recommend and if the father follows through on support
measures ordered or recommended by the Court.

[
6
]

Me Laforce, for the child, consents as well to
the measures proposed by the Director.

[
7
]

The issue before the Court is not so much on the
measures to put in place but rather, on what grounds X's security or
development is compromised.  As we will see, various grounds of
"compromission" were raised: serious behavioural disturbances; sexual
abuse and serious risk of sexual abuse; physical abuse or serious risk of
physical abuse; and psychological ill-treatment.

The facts
prior to the signalements

[
8
]

The parents remained together until the child
was around 3 months old.  During their time together, the father was verbally
violent towards the mother and occasionally physically violent.  He would have
fits of rage over little things.  He was sexually inappropriate with the
mother, having difficulty containing himself and by being very persistent and
harassing.

[
9
]

After the parents' separation, X remained with
her mother but visited her father regularly, although there were frequent
disagreements between parents regarding access.

[
10
]

The mother has a son, Y, from a subsequent
relationship.  Y is about three years younger than X.

[
11
]

The mother is now with a new man with whom she
has a positive relationship.

[
12
]

During the two years prior to April 2011, the
father lived with his girlfriend C.  Ms C has a daughter, Z, who is four years
older than X.  During their time together, X used to visit regularly, about
every second weekend.

[
13
]

Ms C recounted that the father had drug, temper,
violence and sexual problems.  He was addicted to porno and masturbation.  He
often put down the mother (referring to her as a "bitch") and
verbally berated X.  X would sometimes ask her why her father yelled all the
time.  Towards the end of their time together, X expressed no longer wanting to
come for visits.

[
14
]

Ms C also expressed concern that the father may
have sexually abused her daughter Z.  Towards the end of their relationship, Ms
C resorted to placing Z in order to ensure her protection.

[
15
]

Ms C finally fled after a violent incident in
April 2011 following which serious criminal charges were laid against the
father.  He was found guilty of assault and sexual assault and is currently
awaiting sentencing.

[
16
]

In April 2011, mother stopped the child's visits
with her father after hearing that the father was facing charges regarding
sexual abuse regarding Z.  In fact, it was later discovered that the father did
not face charges in relation to Z.  It would appear that this child's version
was too confused for charges to be pressed.

[
17
]

According to the Crown, police found pornography
and cocaine in the father's apartment at the time of their intervention
regarding his girlfriend.

[
18
]

Following April 2011, the father did not have
contact with his daughter.  He called a few times the first year but did not
ask for visits afterwards.

[
19
]

X has stated that she misses her father.

[
20
]

X began presenting behaviour problems at school
during the 2010-2011 school year.  These problems became more severe and
worrisome during the subsequent school year.  She began to act out sexually
with some children, and a shadow was required.

The
evaluation of the signalements

[
21
]

The child's situation was initially signalled in
February 2012 in relation to her inappropriate sexual behaviour.  In March
2012, during investigation of this signalement, X denied having been the victim
of any sexual abuse but stated that she had seen some movies containing sex.
During the investigation, the school reported that X stated that she knows when
her mother is going to "do it".  (D-3, page 4)

[
22
]

In May 2012, she was again signalled in regard
to an isolated incident where the mother would have hit her on the leg.  X and
her mother admitted that there was one incident where the mother hit her
daughter but the DYP concluded that this did not compromise X's security or
development.

[
23
]

Then, in June 2012, the DYP received a third
signalement to the effect that the father and Ms C used to have the child
participate in their sexual relations by having her observe them and by mutual
touching and that X had made sexual advances towards her brother Y.

[
24
]

Ms. [Social Worker 1], behaviour management
specialist with the school board, testified.  She recounted that special
services were requested for X in November 2011 given her problematic sexual and
aggressive behaviour at school and following one incident where she tried
cutting her wrist with scissors.  Ms [Social Worker 1] began working with X in
January 2012.  Ms [Social Worker 1] described various incidents where X
instigated sexual encounters with other girls at school.  In February 2012, X
told her that while visiting her father, she had viewed some pornographic
material.  According to Ms [Social Worker 1], a shadow was hired to follow X
around but nonetheless, there continued to be verbal, physical and sexual
acting-out on the child's part at school.    In early June 2011, the child told
her that having sex made her happy.  She also stated she'd seen her father and
his girlfriend being intimate and that she knew what this meant.  Soon after, a
child care worker ([Social Worker 2]) began following X in and out of class.  X
began making sexual advances to [Social Worker 2].  On June 18, 2012, X told Ms
[Social Worker 1] in [Social Worker 2]'s presence that she tried to have sex
with her brother but that she prefers girls and breasts, particularly adult
breasts.  Asked to explain, X stated that Ms C allowed her to touch and squeeze
her breasts, in the father's absence.  She added however that sometimes, her
father and Ms C would invite her to look at and participate (touch, be touched)
in sex with them in their bed.  While recounting this, the child became aroused
and stated that talking about it made her want to do it.  X asked that they not
report this to anyone else.

[
25
]

During the evaluation of this signalement, X
disclosed that during visits with her father, Ms C would sometimes shower with
her and make her "
wash her all over
".  (D-2, page 7)  She
stated that she had seen her father and Ms C having sex.  She also claimed that
Z would "
get naked and go on her like adults
."

[
26
]

During her testimony before the undersigned, X
repeated that on three or four occasions, she had bathed with Ms C and that Ms C
had asked her to wash her back and breasts and that Ms C had washed all of her
(X's) body.  She stated that she got to not like visiting because of the
baths.  She stated that on one occasion only, she had seen Ms C and her father
naked for a couple of seconds when she opened the door unbeknown to them.  She
stated that there had been one incident with Z taking off her clothes and
kissing her and that Z sometimes put on adult movies.  She acknowledged the one
incident with Y.

[
27
]

Ms C was questioned in Court about what X may
have been exposed to sexually during her visits to their home.  She stated that
it is possible that X may have inadvertently seen pornographic material.  She
denied ever allowing X to watch or participate in any sexual activities with
the father or with her.  Ms C first stated that when she was in the bath or
shower and that X was present, she would always pull the curtain.  A little
later, she acknowledged bathing with X and that they each washed each other.
Rather than deny that X may have washed her (Ms. C's) breasts, Ms C stated that
she does "not remember" any such incident.

[
28
]

The mother did not receive any revelations from
her daughter and was not aware of the incident between her daughter and her
son.  When questioned about her daughter's assertion that she knew when her
mother was going to "do it", the mother stated that she did not know
where this came from and that the child is not exposed to sexual behaviour in
her home.

[
29
]

When contacted by the DYP, the father denied the
allegations, either in relation to his step-daughter or his daughter.  However,
he largely made himself unavailable to discuss his daughter' situation with the
DYP.  On the phone, he is quick to anger.

The facts
subsequent to the signalements

[
30
]

The school had many dealings with the mother in
relation to the child's behaviour.  The school initially questioned the
mother's motivation to get her daughter some help and did not find her
proactive, particularly during the 2011-2012 school year.  They also sometimes had
had difficulty reaching her.

[
31
]

Given her difficulties, X was expelled from [School
A] at the end of the 2011-2012 school year and was referred to the Jewish
General Hospital's Day Treatment Program.  She was accepted into this program
in September 2012.   To get into the program, a Court order was required
because the father refused to sign the authorizations required.

[
32
]

The hospital also encountered certain
difficulties with the mother's commitment (returning calls, attending meetings)
and questioned the mother-daughter relationship to some extent.  For these
reasons, the Hospital was unsure if they would maintain X in their program.

[
33
]

With time, the mother collaborated with the
Hospital.  As DYP reports:  "
It initially took Ms. A time to be
comfortable with the day treatment program but has since proven to be an
insightful and concerned parent
."  (D-6, page 1)  The mother also came
to offer close collaboration with the DYP.

[
34
]

Dr. Jaswant Guzder, head of child psychiatry at
the hospital, reported that from a state of acute distress, X "
was
receptive to support and made rapid gains in social skills within a structured
milieu…
"  However, more work remains to be done.  Indeed, Dr. Guzder's
view is that X's "
precocious exposure to the sexuality, family violence
and disorganized home of her father, and difficulty with disrupted attachments
remain significant focus on ongoing work, as she may seek inappropriate
attention outside her family.  She is both concrete and impulsive, so
structure, consistency, feedback and boundaries will be ongoing supports for
her development.  We have supported her mother in exploring reparation of
bonding and increasing warmth of their attachment
".  (D-5, page 2)

[
35
]

The Hospital also reported that while attending
the program, the father called once demanding a copy of the records.  He seemed
to be intoxicated at the time.  (D-5, page 1)

[
36
]

X was discharged from the hospital program on
November 16, 2012.  She then integrated a new mainstream elementary school, [School
B], and is reportedly doing well.

[
37
]

The mother underwent a parental capacity
assessment with Dr. Niki Saros, psychologist.  This assessment had been deemed
necessary given the concerns raised regarding the mother's ability and
commitment to meet the child's needs.  Dr Saros was asked to "
assess
Ms. A's general mental health and functioning, as it pertains to her capacity
to adequately parent her daughter X.
"  (D-7, page 2)    The assessment
included two meetings with the mother, an observation of the mother with the
child, an interview with the mother, a meeting with DYP and a review of various
reports provided by DYP.  Dr. Saros concluded that the mother "
appears
to be functioning well in her major life roles.  She demonstrates insight
regarding her past parenting problems and acknowledges that her frustrated
reactions to X's behavioural disturbances escalated conflict
."  (D-7,
page 7)  Dr. Saros suggested continued DYP involvement to support the mother in
meeting the child's needs and to provide her with positive parenting strategies.
She recommended that the mother "
attend a support group geared towards
parents of children who have experienced sexual abuse trauma and that X receive
individual counselling for sexual abuse trauma.  X's participation in a support
group for children survivors of trauma may be a helpful supplement to
counselling
."

[
38
]

The mother continued to collaborate well with
the Director.  In January 2013, she began to receive additional supports
through the DYP's Family Preservation Program.  She is also seen as collaborative
with the child's school.

[
39
]

X receives individual psychotherapy at the
Jewish General Hospital and is  progressing well.  Steps have been undertaken
for X to receive therapeutic help from the
Centre A
for which IVAC has
approved funding.  Initial meetings have taken place in order to begin these
services.

New
signalement

[
40
]

On April 11, 2013, it was reported that the
mother hit X in the head.  Both mother and child admit the facts.  Essentially,
the mother got angry, snapped and hit X in the head, hard enough that X hit her
head on the wall and felt dizzy.  The mother explained that "
at times
she feels as though X bullies her brother, as was the case that day.  Ms. A
feels that X seems to be getting so much of the attention lately given
everything that has gone on, that she worries that Y does not get enough
attention and therefore feels very protective of him.  On that day, she was
feeling extremely stressed and overwhelmed as well as frustrated by X's
behaviour and she snapped.  Ms A immediately felt remorseful and guilt ridden
."
(D-9, page 3)

Position
of the parties

[
41
]

As stated at the outset, the issue in this case
concerns grounds for compromission rather than the measures that the Court
should order.  Several grounds of compromission were raised.   These grounds
are defined as follows in section 38 of the Youth Protection Act:

(c) “
psychological
ill-treatment
” refers to a situation in which a child is seriously
or repeatedly subjected to behaviour on the part of the child's parents or
another person that could cause harm to the child, and the child's parents fail
to take the necessary steps to put an end to the situation. Such behaviour
includes in particular indifference, denigration, emotional rejection,
isolation, threats, exploitation, particularly if the child is forced to do
work disproportionate to the child's capacity, and exposure to conjugal or
domestic violence;

(d)
“
sexual
abuse
” refers to

(1)  a situation in which the child is
subjected to gestures of a sexual nature by the child's parents or another
person, with or without physical contact, and the child's parents fail to take
the necessary steps to put an end to the situation; or

(2)  a situation in which the child
runs a serious risk of being subjected to gestures of a sexual nature by the
child's parents or another person, with or without physical contact, and the
child's parents fail to take the necessary steps to put an end to the
situation;

(e)
“
physical abuse
” refers to

(1)  a situation in which the child is
the victim of bodily injury or is subjected to unreasonable methods of
upbringing by his parents or another person, and the child's parents fail to
take the necessary steps to put an end to the situation; or

(2)  a situation in which the child
runs a serious risk of becoming the victim of bodily injury or being subjected
to unreasonable methods of upbringing by his parents or another person, and the
child's parents fail to take the necessary steps to put an end to the
situation;

(f)
“
serious
behavioural disturbance
” refers to a situation in which a child
behaves in such a way as to repeatedly or seriously undermine the child's or
others' physical or psychological integrity, and the child's parents fail to
take the necessary steps to put an end to the situation or, if the child is 14
or over, the child objects to such steps.

[
42
]

The DYP contends that X's security or
development is compromised due to X's
serious behavioural problems
,
which include her sexual acting-out, her self-harm and bullying at school.  The
mother agrees with this as does the child's attorney, the latter pointing out
that these problems would be reactive to the sexual abuse.  The father's lawyer
made no comments on this issue.

[
43
]

The DYP's view is that the two incidents where
the mother hit X constitute "
physical abuse
", particularly
given the severity of the second incident and the fact that many services were
in already in place at that time.  Thus, the DYP feels that this issue needs to
be addressed.  The mother argues that these were isolated incidents and do not
constitute "unreasonable methods of upbringing" as this is not the
way the mother normally raises her child.  The mother further argues that any
risk for further physical discipline is not a "serious risk" and that
this ground should also be set aside.  The father's attorney had no comment to
make on this issue whereas the child's attorney believes that there exists at
least a "serious risk" of physical abuse.

[
44
]

The DYP, the mother and X's attorney believe
that X's security or development is also compromised due to acts of
sexual
abuse
by Ms C and by the father.  They point to the fact that the evidence
regarding Ms C is convincing, particularly in light of X's testimony which, to
a large extent, is corroborated by Ms C herself.  Ms C's actions must be
considered as "sexual abuse" when looked at through the lens of the
child.  They argue that although X did not testify to abuse by the father, she
did not state the opposite and that weight must be given to what she told to
school personnel whom she trusted.  Minimally, there must be a declaration of
"serious risk of sexual abuse" in regard to the father.  The father's
attorney contests any declaration of compromission regarding her client given
that the father denied such, as did Ms C and that the child did not implicate
the father during her testimony.

[
45
]

The child's attorney, during her closing
remarks, argued that X's security or development should also be declared
compromised for "
psychological ill-treatment
" given the
chaotic, violent and denigrating environment X was exposed to while visiting
her father.  The other parties did not respond to this suggestion.

Analysis

[
46
]

X did display
serious behavioural
disturbances
, which included sexual acting-out at school and with her
younger brother, bullying at school and self-harming behaviour.  These
behaviours necessitated DYP, school and psychiatric intervention.

[
47
]

Initially, all professionals involved with the
mother found her to be disconnected to her daughter's needs and slow or
resistant in taking proper action to obtain appropriate help for her.  However,
this could be explained by the mother being overwhelmed by the situation or not
understanding its severity.  The situation improved with time and no longer
presents as a problem.

[
48
]

Nonetheless, to decide on compromission, the
Court must look at the situation at the time the Court was seized of the
situation and at the time, the child was presenting serious behavioural
problems and the mother was not taking the measures to put an end to the
situation.  Thus, the Court will declare
compromission for serious
behavioural disturbances
.

[
49
]

Sexual abuse was raised in relation to Ms C and
in relation to the father.

[
50
]

The
concept of "sexual abuse"

was analyzed by our colleague, the Hon. Carole Brosseau, who, after summarizing
the jurisprudence defining this notion, put it this way:

"
Il
convient de reconnaître que peu importe l'âge de l'enfant, le stade de son
développement et l'intention de la personne qui commet un geste ou prononce une
parole en sa présence ou non, l'abus sexuel peut être défini comme étant toute
atteinte à l'intégrité sexuelle d'un enfant qui résulte de la conduite
sexualisée d'une personne à son égard.  Une atteinte à l'intégrité sexuelle
d'un enfant survient lorsque sa manière d'être, d'agir ou de réagir eu égard à
la sexualité est consciemment ou inconsciemment perturbée.  Quant à la conduite
sexualisée de la personne, on pourrait faire référence à un comportement ou une
attitude avec ou sans geste, toucher ou parole qui peut être qualifié de
sexualisé par toute personne raisonnable."
[1]

[
51
]

Thus, it is from the child's perspective that
the situation must be analyzed in order to determine if the child's sexual
integrity has been affected, taking into consideration the child's age and
development, and not the intentions of the "abuser".

[
52
]

In this particular case, Ms C was someone who
had only known X for a year or two and who only saw her every second weekend or
so.  According to X, on three or four occasions, Ms C bathed with her and
allowed her to wash her (Ms C's) breasts.  Also, during those same baths, Ms C
washed her all over.  This made X feel uncomfortable to the point where she
hesitated to visit.  X testified clearly about all these facts and recounted
them as she had done to the professionals in the past.

[
53
]

Ms C initially testified that she would only
wash herself behind a curtain and finally recognized taking baths with X.  She
was also less than categorical about not allowing X to wash her breasts.
Rather, she stated that she did not remember this.  Thus, the Court believes
that this did take place and given the nature of the acts, the child's age and
her perception and reactions to these baths, they constitute acts of
sexual
abuse by Ms C
towards the child.

[
54
]

The evidence of
sexual abuse
by the
father is less clear.  X only recounted once that her father and Ms C included
her in sexual activities.  X did not testify about sexual gestures by her
father before the Court and when asked, she said she did not remember even
recounting this to Ms [Social Worker 1] but stated that she had told Ms [Social
Worker 1] the truth.  She never spoke to her mother about this.  These
allegations were firmly denied by Ms C and denied by the father.  The child's
allusion to having seen her father and Ms C being intimate could be explained
by her peering through an unlocked door for a few seconds.

[
55
]

On the other hand, it was established that the
father's sexual behaviour with his partners is concerning and that X has
herself displayed very worrisome sexual behaviour.  As well, Ms C raised the
possibility that perhaps her own daughter was sexually abused by the father.

[
56
]

On the whole, the Court is not convinced on a
balance of probabilities that X was sexually abused by her father.  Let us not
forget that X stated that she knew when her mother would be "doing
it", something which does not seem to have a factual basis, at least
according to the mother.  Thus, not all of the child's assertions are
necessarily true.

[
57
]

However, given the concerns enumerated above, in
addition to the child having been exposed to pornographic material while
visiting her father, the court concludes that there is a
serious risk of
sexual abuse by the father
.

[
58
]

In regard to the
physical abuse
, the
facts establish that there were two incidents a year apart where the mother
would have hit X.  The first incident was not serious enough for the DYP to
conclude compromission on, whereas the second incident was.  Further, this
incident second occurred after months of service, including additional supports
by way of an educator.  The child did sustain "bodily injury" and the
mother is taking steps to avoid this from happening again.  Thus, the Court
does not feel that a declaration of compromission is warranted for
"physical abuse".  That said, the mother continues to be under stress
by X's situation and particularly by the fact that X can be aggressive with her
brother.  This is likely to continue and there is a risk, even a serious risk
in the Court's view, that there could be other such incidents, particularly if
this issue is not addressed.  For these reasons, the Court will declare
compromission for "
serious risk of physical abuse
" by her
mother.

[
59
]

Finally, the Court is of the opinion that during
her time visiting her father, the child was subjected to
psychological
ill-treatment
, as invoked by X's attorney.  There were frequent arguments
between the couple, denigration of the mother, lack of respect for X's feelings
and verbal abuse towards Ms A's daughter Z.  In addition, the child was
sexually accosted and exposed to pornographic material by Z.

Corrective
measures

[
60
]

The Court agrees that the mother is very well
able to meet the child's needs and that able to collaborate and follow through
on services required for X.

[
61
]

The father has not demonstrated a willingness to
address his difficulties and has made no efforts to get into contact with his
daughter.

[
62
]

Although X has expressed an interest to see her
father, her situation is fragile and whatever equilibrium presently exists must
not be perturbed.  Two years have passed without contact.  Should the father
want contact with his daughter, he will need to demonstrate to the Court that
such contacts are in his daughter's best interest, taking into consideration
the child's needs and the father's situation.  Thus, the suggestion that
contacts take place if recommended by the therapists at Centre A will not be
retained.

[
63
]

The other measures recommended by the DYP and
agreed to by the parties appear to be in X's best interest.

[
64
]

CONSEQUENTLY, AND FOR THESE REASONS, THE
COURT:

[
65
]

GRANTS
the
motion;

[
66
]

DECLARES
that the
security or development of X is in danger;

[
67
]

IN VIRTUE OF THE POWERS CONFERRED UPON THE
COURT BY SECTION 91 OF THE YOUTH PROTECTION ACT:

[
68
]

ORDERS
that X be
entrusted to her mother;

[
69
]

ORDERS
the mother
to ensure the child is properly supervised in the presence of other children,
including her brother Y;

[
70
]

ORDERS
that the
child be assessed by the [Centre A] and that the recommendations made by
professionals are carried out;

[
71
]

TAKES JUDICIAL NOTICE
that X is to continue individual therapy until  [Centre A]
initiates services;

[
